### 1\. Introduction {#1.-introduction}

The [Climate Connectivity Taxonomy](https://fair2adapt.github.io/climate-connectivity-taxonomy/) drives the climate information visualization tool, the [Climate Connectivity Hub](https://connectivity-hub.weadapt.org/), developed as part of several projects ([PLACARD](https://climate-adapt.eea.europa.eu/en/metadata/projects/platform-for-climate-adaptation-and-risk-reduction),  [MAIA](https://maia-project.eu/)[^1], [Directed](https://directedproject.eu/)[^2] and [FAIR2Adapt](https://fair2adapt-eosc.eu/)[^3]). This note provides background on content, development, users, and usage of Version 1 and next steps of the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy.

**What is the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy?**  
The [Taxonomy](https://fair2adapt.github.io/climate-connectivity-taxonomy/) aims to encourage a standardized approach to knowledge management connecting dispersed climate change knowledge, making it interoperable and reusable, facilitating access to a broad range of audiences. It drives data connections in the [Climate Connectivity Hub](https://connectivity-hub.weadapt.org/?resource=false) and builds on [IPCC AR6 Glossary](https://apps.ipcc.ch/glossary/), the [UNDRR-ISC Hazard Information Profiles](https://www.undrr.org/media/73913/download?startDownload=20250627) and expertly reviewed metadata from the following online platforms: 

* [**CORDIS**](https://cordis.europa.eu/), a comprehensive database of EU Research and Development projects, including those within the climate change and environment domain[^4].  
* [**PreventionWeb**](https://www.preventionweb.net/english/), the knowledge-sharing program of the United Nations Office for Disaster Reduction (UNDRR);  
* [**weADAPT**](http://www.weadapt.org/), the global climate adaptation platform led by the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI).  
* The [**Resilience Platform**](https://resilienceplatform.info/), an online space to capture, access, co-create and advance the latest resilience knowledge;  
* [**Climate-ADAPT**](https://climate-adapt.eea.europa.eu/), the European Climate Adaptation Platform. 

**Who is the Taxonomy for?**

* **Researchers** seeking consistent terminology across studies and datasets.  
* **Data managers** and **website developers** who need to integrate climate vocabularies for enhancing content interoperability and discoverability.  
* **Tool developers** aiming to improve user experience with dynamic term definitions and metadata integration.


  
**How can you use the Climate Connectivity taxonomy?**  
Import the taxonomy via our [API﻿](http://connectivity-hub.com/) (see [Latest version](#latest-version-api)), and explore its use in the [Climate Connectivity Hub](https://connectivity-hub.weadapt.org/?resource=false). Have a go at using the tool and fill out [this survey](https://forms.office.com/e/JsTK4j9acq) to provide feedback which will help improve the Hub and the Taxonomy. 

**How can you contribute to the Climate Connectivity taxonomy?**  
Can’t find the term you’re looking for? Or have a different definition? You can submit a new concept and provide feedback/inputs by contacting [sukaina.bharwani@sei.org](mailto:sukaina.bharwani@sei.org). This may include reflections on how a term is used or perceived in your field, discipline, or professional context which may differ with or add nuance to the definitions and scope notes currently included in the Taxonomy. All feedback will be used to enhance version 1 and shape the development of version 2\.

Embedded in the Climate Connectivity Hub, the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy enhances semantic interoperability, helping tools, platforms, and users speak the same language when navigating climate-related knowledge. 

Before suggesting a new concept, you may want to familiarise yourself with the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy scope (see below).

#### **Latest version API** {#latest-version-api}

##### **Version 1.1, 27 August 2026**  {#version-1.1,-27-august-2026}

Version 1.1: [http\://connectivity-hub.com](http://connectivity-hub.com) 

This version builds on the previous and was developed through the **DIRECTED** and **FAIR2Adapt** projects and includes the development of a **SKOS-supported web tool and repository**, available at [https\://fair2adapt.github.io/climate-connectivity-taxonomy/](https://fair2adapt.github.io/climate-connectivity-taxonomy/). The tool enables users to search, filter and visualise concepts within the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy, with potential for future development of more advanced Boolean and query-based search functionality. 

The update responds to key gaps in existing **climate change adaptation (CCA) vocabularies**, identified primarily through a review of existing taxonomies ([Bharwani et al., 2026](https://www.sei.org/publications/scaling-knowledge-interoperability-for-accelerated-climate-action/)), complemented by ongoing discussions with colleagues and emerging research needs across related projects. The focus was on strengthening concepts that are particularly important for understanding **how and why people and societies adapt, the factors that enable or constrain adaptation, and what adaptation achieves**. 

The revision therefore expanded the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy through the addition of **new concepts, definitions and scope notes**, alongside a more structured network of **broader, narrower and related concept relationships**. In particular, the update strengthened coverage of three areas that were comparatively underdeveloped in existing CCA vocabularies: 

* **Adaptation outcomes and benefits:** capturing what adaptation achieves and the different types of outcomes and benefits that may result;   
* **Adaptation barriers and enablers:** capturing the factors that constrain, facilitate or shape adaptation; and   
* **Adaptation measures and actions:** capturing the interventions, approaches and solutions through which adaptation is implemented. 

Together, these additions strengthen the taxonomy's ability to represent the **relationships between adaptation drivers and context, actions and measures, and resulting outcomes and benefits**, providing a more useful vocabulary for connecting and discovering climate adaptation knowledge.

##### **Version 1.0, 13 June 2025**  {#version-1.0,-13-june-2025}

The Climate Connectivity Taxonomy (v1) is composed of terms from: 1\) existing robust and credible climate change and disaster risk reduction terminologies; 2\) curated thematic terminologies, shaped by project/platform needs and demands; and 3\) ‘tags’ that are used to describe content hosted on online knowledge platforms which are verified and accepted for inclusion by experts. The latter includes pre-existing tags as well as those that have been generated using a large language model (LLM), in the absence of such descriptors. The content of the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy (v1) \- using these three approaches \-  is summarized in the tables below (source: [Bharwani et al., 2026](https://www.sei.org/publications/scaling-knowledge-interoperability-for-accelerated-climate-action/)):

It lists terms alphabetically, with terms linked to related, parent, and child terms where relevant. |

The technical working group used an iterative process of developing and reviewing the hazards listed through extensive consultation with over 500 technical experts from relevant science groups, UN organizations, the private sector, and other partners. The hazard list comprises 302 hazards grouped according to 8 clusters: meteorological and hydrological hazards; extraterrestrial hazards; geohazards; environmental hazards; chemical hazards; biological hazards; technological hazards; and societal hazards. This was complemented by internal consultations and data-generating exercises; literature reviews; and external stakeholder engagement. 140 terms are included in the glossary, 102 related to multi-hazard, multi-risk, disaster risk management and an additional 38 due to their relevance to the project, acknowledging the need for a common understanding amongst an interdisciplinary project consortium covering topics such as research methods. It is organized around three master terms – ‘research’, ‘evaluation’ and ‘study’ – and their typologies. The second level of the taxonomy consists of cross-cutting technical terms – strategies, designs, methods, and outputs – applicable to one or more of the master terms. It provides definitions for all of these terms. |

A co-creation approach was used to refine the scope of the Lexicon. ### 3\. Methodology {#3.-methodology}

   
**The development of the baseline Climate taxonomy**  
The most recent sixth assessment report (AR6) glossary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) and the International Science Council (ISC) Hazard Information Profiles were selected as the basis for the ‘seed taxonomy’: a baseline taxonomy to which selected knowledge structures would subsequently be mapped, given their credibility and robustness in the fields of climate change and disasters respectively.  
   
To complement this, over 35 glossaries or ‘knowledge structures’ (taxonomies, ontologies, and knowledge graphs) were sourced from a diverse range of platforms, including research projects, websites, and academic journals. A preliminary evaluation was conducted to examine the themes, origins, development trajectories, accessibility, and levels of detail of these knowledge structures.  
   
Based on this assessment, 15 datasets were identified as the most pertinent and methodologically robust and were subsequently selected for further analysis within a mapping exercise. Mapping and comparing across the independent knowledge structures was necessary in maximising their complementarity and collective value. Note that taxonomies that were primarily designed and utilized for project or portfolio screening purposes were excluded from this in-depth evaluation.


### 4\. Taxonomy visualization  {#4.-taxonomy-visualization}

### 

**Integration into the Climate Connectivity Hub**   
Following the creation of the baseline taxonomy, a hybrid approach was applied, combining  
automated and manual mapping and analysis to expand and refine the Climate Connectivity taxonomy and dynamically connect content in the Hub. A hybrid approach both increases the efficiency with which large databases can be processed and analyzed and supports the preservation of semantic meanings and nuances. The approach is summarized below and visualized in Figure 1:

* The IPCC glossary and UNDRR taxonomy, and associated meta-data, are imported as the seed taxonomy. This serves as the basis for the Climate Connectivity taxonomy.

* Platform data (e.g. weADAPT, Climate-ADAPT, CORDIS) to be featured on the Hub is  harvested. Identified content expertly curated by knowledge and platform managers, with valuable sets of keywords (terms), these platforms are mapped with and used to enhance the seed taxonomy. A large language model (LLM) is also applied across the platform data to generate new keywords based on text of the ingested content. 

* Both imported and generated keywords are automatically mapped and matched with terms in the seed (or updated, in subsequently iterated) taxonomy using LLM-based text similarity techniques. These new connections dynamically update the visualization of content in the Hub. Keywords imported from knowledge platforms and those generated by the LLM that are unable to be matched with terms from the Climate Connectivity taxonomy become ‘candidate’ terms, which are subject to expert review.

* Candidate keywords can be viewed and manually accepted and/or rejected through the purpose-built admin panel for inclusion in the Climate Connectivity taxonomy; in turn, defining its scope. The order in which candidate keywords are processed is determined based on 1\) frequency (i.e. keywords attached to the most content), or 2\) their inclusion in existing and robust taxonomies (as identified in the collation and mapping exercise) selected to be integrated into the seed taxonomy.

* Meta-data (e.g. definitions, synonyms, related terms) is manually added by topic experts in the taxonomy store to complement or supplement those imported from AR6 and UNDRR and provide additional contextual information.

* All additions of keywords and their associated meta-data are stored and are reflected in an updated taxonomy. The Connectivity Hub is served by an Application Programming Interface (API) that uses the content and meta-data store (MongoDB, PostgreSQL) and the taxonomy store to return a ‘knowledge map’ relevant to the user’s search query (e.g. ‘adaptation’). That is, by importing content assigned to newly accepted terms, the Hub dynamically connects content, keywords, and organizations and returns a visualized ‘knowledge map’ relevant to the users’ search queries.

**The cycle then begins again**, using the updated taxonomy as the new source of keywords and these are re-applied to all existing source platform data. This process enables data to continuously remain connected and thus more discoverable.

### 5\. Next steps {#5.-next-steps}

**Incorporating stakeholder and expert insights in the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy**  
We recognize the diverse ways in which language is applied and understood across different contexts, disciplines, and groups of stakeholders. Work is ongoing to ensure these nuances are captured in the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy through a number of ongoing Horizon Europe projects and Innovation Actions, such as [Directed](https://directedproject.eu/). Version 2 of the Taxonomy will involve deeper engagement on the contextual meaning of Directed Real World Lab-specific climate and disaster risk related vocabulary through semantic analysis of existing documentation and through stakeholder engagement.

### 6\. Appendix {#6.-appendix}

**Using a Large Language Model to support taxonomy development**    
Figure 2 provides a specific example illustrating the journey of a single content entity – an article on "New Methods Linking City Design and Sustainable Urban Agriculture Practices" and the application of the Large Language Model (LLM). This visualization demonstrates how content is analyzed, linked to the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy, and contributes to its growth via candidate term generation and review (source: [Bharwani et al., 2026](https://www.sei.org/publications/scaling-knowledge-interoperability-for-accelerated-climate-action/)). 

![][image2]  
**Figure 2: The journey of a hypothetical piece of content through the taxonomy curation process (source: [Bharwani et al., 2026](https://www.sei.org/publications/scaling-knowledge-interoperability-for-accelerated-climate-action/)).**   
   
 

**Figure 2.1 (Arrival):** The example article is ingested into the system. It arrives with a pre-existing source keyword ('city farming') associated with it. 

**Figure 2.2 (Content Analysis & AI Keywords Appear):** The system processes the ingested content. Firstly, as part of the mapping efforts, the textual content itself is analyzed for conceptual links to the existing Climate Connectivity Taxonomy. In this instance, a link to the 'Sustainability' term is established. Secondly, corresponding to Step 3 of the overall process, Large Language Model (LLM) techniques are employed to extract relevant keywords directly from the article's text, independent of source tags. Here, the AI generates 'urban agriculture', 'rooftop gardens', 'City Design', and 'Vertical Farming'. These keywords are now associated with the content item alongside its source keyword. 

**Figure 2.3 (Keyword Mapping & Candidate Generation):** All associated keywords ('city farming', 'urban agriculture', 'rooftop gardens', 'City Design', 'Vertical Farming') are checked against the current CC Taxonomy and the existing candidate term list using LLM-based semantic similarity matching. 

* A match is found for the AI keyword 'City Design', which is mapped to the existing Taxonomy term 'Urban Planning'.   
* A match is found for the AI keyword 'Vertical Farming', which is mapped to an existing term within the candidate term list. Keywords that do not find a suitable match ('city farming', 'urban agriculture', 'rooftop gardens') become potential new candidate terms. Synonym detection, potentially part of the similarity analysis, identifies 'city farming' and 'urban agriculture' as synonyms; 'urban agriculture' is chosen as the representative term and suggested as a single new candidate for this group. The remaining unmapped keyword, 'rooftop gardens', is suggested as an individual new candidate Term. 

**Figure 2.4 (Review & Taxonomy Update):** This figure reflects the expert curation process. The newly generated Candidate Terms ('urban agriculture', 'rooftop gardens') are presented to experts for review. In this example, 'urban agriculture' is approved, while 'rooftop gardens' is rejected. The single approved term is then formally integrated into the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy, permanently enriching it. 

**Figure 2.5 (Final User View):** This final figure illustrates the outcome for the end-user, representing the dynamic 'knowledge map' presentation. The original article is now displayed with explicit links to the relevant terms within the finalized CC Taxonomy. The figure highlights the provenance of these links, demonstrating the different pathways through which categorization occurred: 

* The link to 'Sustainability' was derived directly from the initial Content Analysis.   
* The link to 'Urban Planning' resulted from the AI Keyword 'City Design' being directly mapped to that Taxonomy term.   
* The link to 'urban agriculture' was established because the synonym group ('city farming'/'urban agriculture') generated a candidate term that was subsequently approved by experts and added to the Taxonomy. 

(Note: As per the clarification that only terms formally in the Climate Connectivity Taxonomy contribute to the final user view, the link established via the keyword 'Vertical Farming' mapping to an *existing candidate* in Figure 2.3 is not shown here, as that candidate was not depicted as being formally approved and added to the main Climate Connectivity Taxonomy in this specific example flow.) 

This demonstrates how the cyclical process connects content through multiple analysis and curation layers, providing rich, traceable links within the dynamically updated knowledge Hub.
